'''Andrew Perry Ingersoll''' (born 1940) is an American physicist. He is a professor of [[planetary science]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]]. Ingersoll was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1997.<ref>{{Cite web |title=American Academy of Arts and Sciences Fellows |url=http://m.caltech.edu/content/american-academy-arts-and-sciences-fellows |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181215224732/http://m.caltech.edu/content/american-academy-arts-and-sciences-fellows |archive-date=2018-12-15 |access-date=2018-12-13 |website=Caltech}}</ref> He received the lifetime achievement award in planetary science, the [[Gerard P. Kuiper Prize]], in 2007. He proposed the [[runaway greenhouse effect]] and is known for his research on planetary atmospheres and climate.

==Biography==
He was born in [[Chicago, Illinois]], in 1940 and moved to Brooklyn as a child, graduating from high school there at age 16. He received his bachelor's degree from [[Amherst College]] in 1960 and his master's degree from Harvard in 1961. He received his Ph.D. of [[Physics]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1966, focusing on [[geophysical fluid dynamics]].

After his graduation, he joined [[Caltech]] as an assistant professor in the Planetary Science department in 1966. He became an associate professor in 1971 and a full professor in 1976. He was the Earle C. Anthony Professor of [[Planetary science|Planetary Science]] at Caltech from 2003 to 2011. He has made significant contributions to understanding planetary atmospheres, including fundamental studies on the runaway greenhouse effect on [[Venus]], and [[atmospheric physics]] on [[giant planet]]s and the Earth.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Team|url=https://www.missionjuno.swri.edu/the-team|website=Mission Juno|publisher=Southwest Research Institute|accessdate=22 November 2015}}</ref>

He has been a leader in the investigation of planetary weather and [[climate]], particularly on giant planets and the Earth, for nearly five decades. He has been a key player on the instrument teams for many NASA/[[Jet Propulsion Laboratory|JPL]] missions, including [[Pioneer Venus project|Pioneer Venus]], [[Pioneer 10|Pioneer Saturn]], [[Voyager program|Voyager]], [[Mars Global Surveyor]], [[Galileo project|Galileo]], and [[Cassini–Huygens|Cassini]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Andrew Ingersoll - Earle C. Anthony Professor of Planetary Science, California Institute Technology |url=http://www.planetary.org/connect/our-experts/profiles/andrew-ingersoll.html |website=The Planetary Society}}</ref>

He has been interviewed about his research on the [[Science Channel]] documentary "[[The Planets and Beyond|The Planets]]". He is the author of the book ''Planetary Climates''.<ref>{{cite book|title=Planetary Climates|url=https://press.princeton.edu/titles/10160.html|last=Ingersoll|first=Andrew|date=25 August 2013|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=9780691145044}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
Among many other awards, he received the [[Gerard P. Kuiper Prize]] for outstanding lifetime achievement in planetary science in 2007, the [[NASA Exceptional Scientific Achievement Medal]] in 1981 for his work on the [[Voyager program]], and was elected as a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1997.<ref>{{cite press release |author=Kathy Svitil  |title=Caltech's Ingersoll Receives Achievement Award |url=http://www.caltech.edu/news/caltechs-ingersoll-receives-achievement-award-1330 |location=[[Pasadena, California]] |publisher= Caltech |agency=[[California Institute of Technology]]|date=2007-10-10 |access-date=2017-04-09}}</ref>

He was elected a Legacy Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]] in 2020.<ref>{{cite web |title=AAS Fellows Program |url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/aas-fellows |accessdate=29 September 2020 |publisher=American Astronomical Society}}</ref>
